This is the un-optimized shader. It hasn't run through dead code elimination yet. So it's expected that it would contain the entire shader template. 

All shaders go through a dead code elimination step during compilation. So this is nothing to be worried about

The native shader code visualization just inserts your GDShader code into our shader template and displays it for you in GLSL. No optimizations are done on it. 

Just looking at that code alone tells you nothing. You need to actually profile the code to see what parts are taking time and where your bottlenecks are. 

The tonemap shader is an interesting observation. In 4.6 I optimized the mobile tonemap shader to remove all that branching and got a nice speed boost on mobile devices. It didn't really impact desktop devices though, as expected.

That gets completely removed since it is dead code. 

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead-code_elimination

When compiling a shader, the compiler starts from the output and goes backwards. The only code that gets included in the final binary is code that contributes to the final output. 

With the roughness limiter example above the entire branch is removed since roughness doesn't contribute to the final output. 

Again, don't waste your time trying to guess what the compiler will and won't do. If you profile an unshaded shader using a GPU profiler you will see that no work is being done in the fragment shader. Trying to speculate by looking at a high level shader language is a waste of everyone's time

Thanks @clayjohn. I'm not arguing, just trying to understand. 

E.g. why do you think any of that branching based on uniforms is even going to be considered a dead code in the first place? Given that uniform values may change any frame...
